research.title: Research — Ben Silver
research.description: Mass cytometry at Mass General's Vaccine and Immunotherapy Center, and flexible bioelectronics at Sonkusale Research Labs.
research.heading: Research
research.lead: Two labs so far, both asking a version of the same question: can you trust what the instrument just told you, and can anyone else reproduce it tomorrow.

positions.name: Mass cytometry at the Vaccine & Immunotherapy Center
bullets: Immune populations across vaccine stimulations can now be called from a reproducible Python pipeline rather than by hand, on datasets past a million events.
Raw instrument output reaches usable populations in a single pass, because FCS parsing, arcsinh transformation and dimensionality reduction were built into one path instead of three manual steps.
Cluster assignments hold up to immunological review rather than merely looking clean, after biological validation metrics were added to the existing clustering.

New cohorts start from the pipeline instead of from scratch: X-shift surfaces where cell population abundance has moved, and the Shannon and Simpson diversity notebooks written for the first project carry straight across, at the same million-cell scale.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: Fifty-plus parameters per cell, past a million events per dataset

facts.label: Method
facts.value: Python, NumPy, scikit-learn, FlowSOM, OMIQ, UMAP and PCA

positions.name: Flexible electrode arrays at Sonkusale Research Labs
paragraphs: Gave the group fabrication protocols they could repeat, by characterising the signal across physiological conditions on the bench until the failure points were known rather than guessed. The lesson carried: a measurement is only ever as good as the thing taking it.
It is also where I learned to be useful in a wet lab. Protocol and safety first, which is what earns you the bench time to try anything at all.

facts.label: Domain
facts.value: Flexible bioelectronics for wearable, point-of-care diagnostics

projects.title: Projects — Ben Silver
projects.description: CraveCast, a craving forecaster for addiction recovery, and EpiAlert, allergen detection and epinephrine mapping for travellers.
projects.heading: Projects
projects.lead: Both of these started because someone I know had a problem that software could plausibly help with, and neither of them is a demo.

items.name: CraveCast
paragraphs: People in recovery get a warning before a craving lands rather than a record of it afterwards, forecast from their own logs and the peer-reviewed ADARP study.

The forecast is kernel density estimation over the hours somebody has actually logged a craving, read against the population-level risk windows in the study, so it is useful on the first day and personal by the second week. It runs entirely in the browser and works with the network off, so nothing about a person's recovery leaves their device. Building it is where I learned what it takes to get a published model to actually run: choosing the bandwidth, deciding what counts as a signal, and working out how you would know whether a prediction was any good.

It started at a lung transplant observership at Mass General. COPD is one of the most common reasons somebody ends up needing new lungs, and smoking is the leading cause of COPD. Watching what people went through before, during and after that operation is why I wanted to build something for the addiction end of it rather than the surgical end.

The other half of it is that it should be worth opening. Recovery apps tend to be either a logbook or a clinical dashboard, and nobody wants either at the moment they need one. This one has streaks and unlocks and some colour, because breaking an addiction is hard enough without the tool being another chore.

facts.label: Built with
facts.value: HTML, JavaScript, Python, kernel density estimation

items.name: EpiAlert
paragraphs: A photograph of a meal becomes an allergen decision in seconds, with the nearest stocked epinephrine on the same screen.

I grew up in Taiwan with a nut allergy. By now I know that pad thai usually has crushed peanuts in it and that a lot of Indian curries are thickened with cashews, but a shy nine-year-old has none of that and is not going to ask a waiter. This is the check I did not have.

It is a first check and not a verdict, and the app says so. The point is the unfamiliar meal in a country where you cannot be sure the waiter understood the question — enough to settle it, or to tell you this is one to ask about properly. It remembers what you are allergic to, and it is simple enough that a kid could use it at the table.
I cut a peer-review feed late on, once it was clear that crowd-sourced safety data is a liability when the failure mode is anaphylaxis.

facts.label: Built with
facts.value: Python, Flask, Claude Vision API, Google Maps API

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Repository private, happy to walk through it

about.title: About — Ben Silver
about.description: Computer science and biology at Tufts, research computing at Tufts Technology Services, and where Ben Silver would like this to go next.
about.heading: About
paragraphs: I came to Tufts for computer science and added a focus in biological sciences once it turned out the biology was the part I couldn't stop reading about. Those two things looked unrelated for about a year and then stopped being unrelated at all.

I grew up in a Taiwanese-American household, which is where I learned that the answer to most questions is to take the lid off and look. That habit is more or less the whole story: a bike that shifts badly gets stripped to the frame, a knife that won't bite gets a whetstone and an argument about angles, and a dataset with a million immune cells in it gets a pipeline until the clusters mean something.

At Tufts Technology Services I look after tooling for research storage. The old request workflow had staff retyping the same details into a fixed format by hand; mine takes a paste, picks the template for the kind of request being handled, and formats it. About a quarter of the time back on each one, a single consistent format at the end of it, and nothing for a new starter to memorise.

Data is one big haystack and computer science is the magnet. That is most of why I like this: finding the pattern, and then getting it in front of somebody who can act on it. Biotech and healthcare data are where I would most like that to land, though the part I actually care about — prediction, patterns, making numbers usable — travels anywhere data does.

feature.note: I draw the patterns myself and prototype them in paper first, because leather does not forgive a measurement you guessed at. Most of what got better between those two wallets is that I stopped guessing.

second.name: Bikes, mostly in pieces
second.blurb: I ride mountain bikes, and the half I like best is the one where the bike is on the floor in pieces. Brakes bled and upgraded, a dropper post fitted, headset and gears dialled in, a new cassette — most of what is on mine now, I put there. Down to cable ends that match the frame, which nobody notices but me.
